title: Ten of These Is One of Those

steps.body: The spots run a **trading post** with one rule: 10 ones = 1 ten, and 10 tens = 1 hundred. Trades work both directions. This single rule secretly powers carrying, borrowing, and the ×10 shift you met in the fluency chapter — it's the engine under all of arithmetic.
Trade up: loose ones into tens.

widget.prompt: 60 loose beads get traded into bags of 10. Slide the number of bags until every bead is bagged.
widget.lowFeedback: Loose beads remain — every bag swallows exactly 10 more. Add a bag.
widget.highFeedback: You're bagging more than 60 beads now — take one bag away; each holds 10.
widget.successFeedback: 6 bags of 10 hold exactly 60 — sixty ones traded into 6 tens. Same beads, new packaging.

predict.prompt: 60 loose beads get bagged in tens. How does the number of bags relate to the digits of 60?
predict.reveal: Bags of ten ARE the tens place — 60 holds six tens, so six bags swallow every bead. The tens digit counts the bags.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents unit trading.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for unit trading must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines unit trading.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

steps.body: The trading post's golden rule: value never changes.
explanationVariants: He hands IN 10 ones and receives 1 ten — the ten replaces them: 1 ten + 4 ones = 14, same as before.
Count the value both ways: before, 14 ones; after, 10 + 4. The packaging changed; the amount didn't.

widget.prompt: Kai has 14 loose ones. He trades 10 of them for 1 ten. What does he hold now?

options.label: 1 ten and 4 ones — still worth 14
options.feedback: The 10 ones LEFT his hands when the ten arrived. New packaging, same value: 14.

options.label: 1 ten and 14 ones — worth 24 now
options.feedback: That keeps the ten AND the traded ones — counting them twice! A trade hands the 10 ones over; only 4 stay loose.

options.label: Just 4 ones — the trade shrank his money
options.feedback: The 4 loose ones remain, but the 1 ten he received is worth the missing 10. Trades never shrink value.

options.label: 2 tens
options.feedback: 2 tens would be worth 20 — but Kai only brought 14 to the post. He can afford one ten, with 4 ones left loose.

steps.body: Trades run **downhill too**: 1 hundred breaks into 10 tens, and 1 ten breaks into 10 ones. That's where "borrowing" in subtraction really comes from — you're not borrowing, you're trading a big unit down into small change.
Break big units into small change.
explanationVariants: Each hundred breaks into 10 tens, so 3 hundreds break into 3 × 10 = 30 tens.
Check the value: 30 tens = 300 — exactly what 3 hundreds were worth. The trade preserved it.

widget.prompt: 3 hundreds are traded down entirely into tens. How many tens?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 forgot the trading rate — EACH hundred breaks into 10 tens, not 1. Three hundreds make three sets of 10 tens.
300 traded all the way down to ONES. Stop one level up: in tens, 3 hundreds make 30.
13 adds 3 + 10 — but trading multiplies: each of the 3 hundreds becomes 10 tens.

widget.fallbackFeedback: One hundred = 10 tens. Do that trade three times.

widget.prompt: Match each packaging to its value. Some packagings hide a trade inside!

pairErrors.feedback: 1 ten + 16 ones is 10 + 16 = 26, not 32 — the 16 ones hide an extra ten inside, but that only brings it to 2 tens 6 ones.

widget.missFeedback: Add each packaging's value: tens are worth 10 each, hundreds 100. Non-standard packs still total honestly.
widget.successFeedback: 26, 32, 150 — packaging can look strange, but the value always adds up the same.

explanationVariants: 2 tens (20) plus 13 ones: 20 + 13 = 33. The 13 ones could trade into 1 ten 3 ones, making the tidy form 3 tens 3 ones.
Trade first if you like: 13 ones = 1 ten + 3 ones, so altogether 3 tens 3 ones = 33.

widget.prompt: A jar holds 2 tens and 13 ones. What number is that?

commonErrors.feedback: 213 glued the packaging labels together. Add the VALUES instead: 2 tens are 20, plus the 13 ones.
23 read the 13 ones as just 3 — but 13 ones hide a whole extra ten inside. Count all of them: 20 + 13.
15 added the labels (2 + 13), ignoring what a ten is worth. Each ten counts as 10: 20 + 13.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Value it out: 2 tens = 20, then add all 13 ones.

steps.body: A bank teller's trade, step by step.
hints: First the trade: ONE hundred breaks down into how many tens?
The tens drawer now holds 10 tens (it started empty).
Then 2 tens are given away. How many stay in the drawer?
explanationVariants: Trade: 1 hundred → 10 tens in the drawer. Give away 2: 10 − 2 = 8 tens remain.
Only the traded hundred feeds the tens drawer; after the giveaway it keeps 8 tens (worth 80).

widget.prompt: A bank drawer holds 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones. The teller trades ONE hundred down into tens, then gives away 2 tens. How many tens are in the drawer now?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 is the drawer right after the trade — the giveaway hasn't happened yet. Hand over the 2 tens.
38 counts the bank's WHOLE value in tens (380 = 38 tens). The question asks only what sits in the tens drawer: the traded 10, minus 2.
2 is what LEFT the drawer. The drawer received 10 tens from the trade and gave 2 away — count what stayed.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two moves: one hundred becomes 10 tens; then 2 of those walk out the door.

steps.body: You run the trading post now.
takeaways: 10-for-1 trades go up (bundle) and down (break) between neighboring spots.
Trades change packaging, never value — count it both ways to prove it.
Carrying and borrowing are just these trades wearing school clothes.
steps.teaser: next chapter: every number has two neighbors — rounding finds the closer one.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Think **bundles of sticks**: 10 loose sticks snap into 1 bundle; 10 bundles pack into 1 box. Loose = ones, bundles = tens, boxes = hundreds. Trading never adds or loses a single stick — it only regroups them.

explanationVariants: 10 bundles of 10 sticks hold 100 sticks — exactly one box: a hundred.
Ten tens are worth 10 × 10 = 100, the next spot up.

options.label: 1 hundred
options.feedback: Ten bundles of ten pack into one box: 10 tens = 1 hundred.

options.label: 1 ten
options.feedback: One ten is what you started EACH bundle as. Ten of them together climb a whole spot: a hundred.

options.label: 100 hundreds
options.feedback: That would be 10,000 sticks! Ten tens are worth 100 — exactly one hundred, not a hundred of them.
